systemPrompt:
You are an educational designer planning an interactive guided demo for a 2D textbook figure.

INTERACTION PALETTE — choose the interactions that best fit the concept. Pick the fewest that genuinely serve the learning goal; more is not better. In "teaches", say what the learner understands, not what the control does.

• orbit / drag — rotate/move the scene. When depth or 3D shape IS the concept.
• hover — reveal a label on demand. When showing every label at once clutters.
• click — highlight one element. When focus on one part of a busy scene matters.
• slider — sweep one continuous variable. When dragging it visibly transforms the figure.
• toggle — switch between 2+ named views. For before/after or dual views (e.g. spatial ↔ frequency).
• button / state — step through discrete phases. When distinct stages should be visited deliberately.
• animation — self-playing motion. When the concept is inherently dynamic and a slider can't convey it.
• equation_input — learner types math, parsed at runtime. When "change the formula, reshape the output" (integrand, boundary, kernel); each field maps to one curve/quantity; catch parse errors inline.
• code_editor — learner writes/debugs an algorithm; the figure replays its execution frame by frame. Use ONLY when the concept IS a procedure whose intermediate states carry the lesson — heapify, one pass of a sort, a graph traversal, gradient descent, scanline fill — i.e. the question a learner has is "in what order does it touch the data, and why". Needs state small enough to draw whole (~30 elements) and an algorithm expressible in ~20 lines against a handful of operations. Do NOT use it for a continuous parameter (that is a slider), a formula the learner retypes (equation_input), or a static structure with no execution (hover/click). Choose it over animation when the learner should be able to get the procedure WRONG and watch where it diverges.

Output ONLY this JSON (no markdown, no explanation):
{
  "concept": "One sentence: the core concept this figure teaches.",
  "figureType": "line_plot | scatter_plot | bar_chart | flow_chart | network_diagram | diagram | other",
  "elements": ["exhaustive list of every visual element to reconstruct — axes, data series, nodes, edges, labels, annotations, legends"],
  "interactions": [
    { "id": "camelCaseId", "type": "orbit | drag | hover | click | slider | toggle | button | state | animation | equation_input | code_editor", "teaches": "what the learner understands", "...": "plus ONLY that type's fields per INTERACTION FIELDS below" }
  ],
  "demo_steps": [
    {
      "title": "Step name shown in UI",
      "narration": "What the learner sees and understands at this step — one or two sentences",
      "state": { "interactionId": value }
    }
  ],
  "keyInsight": "The single most important 'aha moment' — the thing that makes this concept click.",
  "reconstructionNotes": "High-level visual description for the generator: approximate layout, colors, key labels, data patterns, important annotations. No pixel measurements — describe what matters visually."
}

INTERACTION FIELDS — every interaction object has "id" (unique camelCase), "type", and "teaches". Add ONLY the fields listed for its type; never attach a "range" to anything but a slider.

"type" MUST be exactly one of these 11 strings: "orbit" · "drag" · "hover" · "click" · "slider" · "toggle" · "button" · "state" · "animation" · "equation_input" · "code_editor""

• orbit / drag / hover / click — no extra fields.
• animation      — "label", optional "loop": true | false.
• slider         — "label", "range": [min, max, step], "default": <number>.
• toggle         — "label", "options": ["A", "B", ...], "default": "A"   (a plain on/off toggle may drop "options" and use "default": true | false).
• button / state — "label", "states": ["idle", "running", "done"], "default": "idle".
• equation_input — "label", "fields": [ { "id": "...", "label": "f(x) =", "default": "sin(x)", "variables": ["x"], "domain": [min, max], "role": "integrand | boundary | kernel | ..." } ]. "domain" is the x-range the field is plotted over; always supply it so the generator does not have to guess.
• code_editor    — "label",
                   "entry_point": "the one function the learner must define, e.g. buildMaxHeap(heap)",
                   "api": [ { "op": "greater(i, j)", "does": "true when A[i] > A[j]" }, { "op": "swap(i, j)", "does": "exchange two elements — the ONLY way to mutate" }, ... ],
                   "frame": "what one recorded step shows, e.g. 'the whole array plus the 1-2 indices the op touched'",
                   "input": { "label": "Initial array", "default": "4, 1, 3, 2, 16, 9, 10" },
                   "sample_code": "<correct implementation, as a string>",
                   optional "buggy_code": "<plausible near-miss, with a comment naming the bug>",
                   "success_check": "the property the final state must satisfy, e.g. 'every parent >= both of its children'".
  Design the "api" first and keep it minimal: 4–7 ops covering read, compare, mutate, and annotate (a note/mark op for the learner's own commentary). Every state change must be reachable ONLY through an op — otherwise the replay has gaps. The learner writes algorithm logic, never drawing code.

demo_steps "state" may set values for slider, toggle, and button/state interactions only; code_editor and equation_input are seeded by their sample_code / fields defaults, not by demo_steps.

2D-SPECIFIC RULES:
- figureType: pick the closest match; used only to select the rendering library (flow_chart → Mermaid, plots → Chart.js, everything else → SVG.js).
- elements: list every distinct visual element the generator needs to recreate — every axis, every data series by name/color, every node/edge, every annotation.
- interactions: orbit/drag are valid if the figure benefits from pan/zoom; animation is valid for process or sequence diagrams. OrbitControls is NOT available in 2D — orbit means pan/zoom the SVG viewport, not 3D rotation.
- code_editor is fully available in 2D and is often the RIGHT choice in array/tree/graph figures that illustrate an algorithm (heapify, a sort pass, BFS/DFS, scanline fill) are 2D figures whose lesson is the execution order, not the picture. Pair it with figureType "diagram" or "network_diagram" — never "flow_chart" or a plot type, since those route to renderers that cannot redraw an arbitrary structure per frame. When you pick code_editor, make it the figure's primary interaction rather than adding it alongside several sliders.
- demo_steps: include when the concept has 2+ distinct phases. Each step state sets interaction values. Use [] if the figure is a single static view with no natural sequence.
- keyInsight: one sentence. The thing you most want the student to walk away remembering.
- reconstructionNotes: describe what matters for faithful recreation — axis labels, approximate data shape, color coding, key annotations — but do NOT enumerate exact data coordinates.
- Output ONLY valid JSON — no markdown fences, no explanation.

userContent.text:
Figure: "CNX_UPhysics_18_05_PhaseDiag" (chapter: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 18: Temperature and Heat)

Planner context:
This figure is a single pressure-temperature plot headed H2O. The vertical axis reads "Pressure, p (atm)" with ticks at 0.006, 1, and 218, and the horizontal axis reads "Temperature, T (C)" with ticks at 0, 0.01, 100, and 374, the spacing on both visibly nonlinear. Two red curves meet at a filled dot labeled "Triple point" at 0.006 atm and 0.01 degrees, with dashed guide lines running to both axes. From that dot one branch rises almost vertically and leans slightly left, while the other sweeps up and to the right, ending at a second filled dot labeled "Critical point" at 218 atm and 374 degrees; below the triple point a single curve continues toward the lower left. Italic letters mark the regions the curves carve out: s at the left, l in the wedge between the branches, and v at the right. Curved arrows tag the branches "Melting", "Boiling", and "Sublimation", and a dashed pair marks the crossing at 1 atm and 100 degrees. Locating a point against these curves tells the reader which phase water occupies there. The plot lays out the coexistence boundaries, including the leftward-leaning melting line whose negative slope means added pressure can melt ice.

AUTHOR-PROVIDED INTERACTION REQUESTS:
Requested interactions:
- Slider for temperature and pressure: the learner adjusts T and p controls, a state point moves across the diagram and the solid, liquid, or vapor region highlights, making clear that phase is determined by location relative to the coexistence curves.
- Slider for pressure near the melting boundary: the learner raises pressure along a fixed-temperature line close to 0 degrees C, the state point crosses the left-leaning melting curve and the phase label changes from solid to liquid, making clear why added pressure can melt ice.
- Toggle between heating paths: the learner switches among a 1 atm path, a low-pressure path through the triple point area, and a supercritical path, the crossed boundaries and transition labels appear, making clear how boiling, sublimation, and the critical point depend on the path through p-T space.

Source file:
OpenStax University Physics, chapter 18: Temperature and Heat

Use these requested interactions when forming the plan. Use the image to recover visual structure, layout, labels, camera/view cues, and missing visible elements.

Design an educational guided demo for this figure and return the pedagogical blueprint as JSON.

Build an interactive figure using Chart.js.

CONCEPT: A pressure–temperature phase diagram partitions p–T space into solid, liquid, and vapor regions separated by coexistence curves, so a substance's phase is determined entirely by where its state point falls relative to those curves.
KEY INSIGHT (what students should walk away understanding): A phase is not set by temperature alone — it is set by the location of the (T, p) point relative to the coexistence curves, which is why water's backward-leaning melting line lets pressure alone turn ice into liquid.
DEMO STEPS: 5 guided steps — implement the step player in #ui

FULL BLUEPRINT:

    "Red sublimation curve rising from the lower-left origin region up to the triple point",

    "Red vaporization (boiling) curve sweeping up and right from the triple point to the critical point",

        1

      "default": 25

    {
      "id": "pressure",
      "type": "slider",
      "teaches": "Moving vertically at fixed temperature can change phase too — raising pressure just below 0 °C pushes the state point across the left-leaning melting curve from solid into liquid, which is why pressure melts ice.",
      "label": "Pressure, log₁₀ p (atm)",
      "range": [
        -3,
        2.5,
        0.05
      ],
      "default": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "heatingPath",
      "type": "toggle",

    }
  ],
  "demo_steps": [
    {
      "title": "Read the map",
      "narration": "The state point sits at room conditions (25 °C, 1 atm) and the liquid region lights up. Phase is not a property of temperature alone — it is a location on this map.",
      "state": {
        "temperature": 25,
        "pressure": 0,
        "heatingPath": "Free explore"
      }
    },
    {
      "title": "Heat water at 1 atm",
      "narration": "Follow the horizontal 1 atm path from -20 °C upward in temperature. The path crosses the melting curve near 0 °C and the boiling curve at exactly 100 °C — the familiar transitions are just two curve crossings.",

        "temperature": 130,
        "pressure": 0,
        "heatingPath": "1 atm heating"
      }
    },
    {
      "title": "Drop below the triple point",
      "narration": "At 0.002 atm — below the triple-point pressure of 0.006 atm — the horizontal path misses the liquid wedge entirely and crosses only the sublimation curve. Solid goes straight to vapor; liquid water cannot exist.",
      "state": {
        "temperature": 60,
        "pressure": -2.7,
        "heatingPath": "Low pressure (0.002 atm)"
      }
    },
    {
      "title": "Squeeze ice until it melts",
      "narration": "Hold the temperature just below 0 °C and raise the pressure. Because the melting curve leans left, climbing vertically carries the state point from solid into liquid — added pressure melts ice.",
      "state": {
        "temperature": -2,
        "pressure": 1.9,
        "heatingPath": "Free explore"
      }
    },
    {
      "title": "Above the critical point",
      "narration": "At 250 atm the path passes above the critical point and no boiling curve remains to cross. Liquid and vapor merge continuously into a single supercritical fluid.",
      "state": {
        "temperature": 420,
        "pressure": 2.4,
        "heatingPath": "Supercritical (250 atm)"
      }
    }
  ],
  "keyInsight": "A phase is not set by temperature alone — it is set by the location of the (T, p) point relative to the coexistence curves, which is why water's backward-leaning melting line lets pressure alone turn ice into liquid.",
  "reconstructionNotes": "Single quadrant plot with arrowheaded axes, white background, thin black axes and dashed black guide lines, and the three coexistence curves drawn in a single medium red stroke. Both axes are strongly nonlinear (log-like) so that 0.006, 1 and 218 atm and 0, 0.01, 100 and 374 °C are all comfortably spaced; the origin region sits at the lower left. The sublimation curve rises gently from near the origin to the triple-point dot at (0.01 °C, 0.006 atm); from there the melting curve shoots almost straight up while drifting slightly LEFT (this leftward lean must be visually obvious — it is the lesson), and the vaporization curve arcs up and to the right, steepening, ending at the critical-point dot at (374 °C, 218 atm). Both special points are filled black dots with leader-free text labels ('Triple point' below-right of its dot, 'Critical point' above-right of its dot). Italic single-letter region labels s (left of the melting line), l (in the tall wedge), v (right of the boiling curve). Three hand-drawn-style curved arrows enter from outside the plot labeled 'Melting' (upper left), 'Boiling' (right, mid-height), 'Sublimation' (lower left). Interactive additions: a state-point marker (bold open circle with dot) plus a small readout box showing T, p, and the phase word; the enclosing phase region gets a soft translucent fill (blue-grey for solid, blue for liquid, warm yellow for vapor, purple wash above critical p+T) whenever the point is inside it. When a heating path is selected, draw a dashed horizontal arrow at that pressure spanning the temperature range, with small vertical tick marks and text labels ('melting', 'boiling', 'sublimation', or 'no transition — supercritical') at each red-curve crossing."
}
